impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when assessing copyright infringement damages, and what constitutes a permissible 'book of wisdom' analysis in a hypothetical negotiation for government copyright infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's use of a hypothetical negotiation to assess damages for the government's infringement of copyrighted software (TETRA®), rather than deferring to the existing license agreement terms. However, it vacated the damages award in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. The case establishes important guardrails for copyright damages methodology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's endorsement of the hypothetical negotiation methodology, which may yield higher damages than existing license rates. The decision confirms flexibility in choosing damages models.
impacts.negativeImplications: The court's restriction on the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and prohibition on non-compensatory damages limits the ability of copyright holders to maximize recovery, particularly in government infringement cases under 28 U.S.C. § 1498.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling based on a prior class action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that § 2501's statute of limitations is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. implicitly overruled the Federal Circuit's prior contrary holding in Bright v. United States. Banks and their holding companies that invested Tier 1 Capital in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac preferred shares and lost assets during the 2008 financial crisis were time-barred from bringing takings and breach of contract claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: The decision provides certainty for the government and financial regulators that stale claims arising from the 2008 financial crisis cannot be revived through American Pipe tolling, limiting open-ended litigation exposure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Financial institutions and investors who relied on pending class actions to toll their individual claims against the government face permanent loss of their causes of action. This narrows the window for filing individual takings claims significantly.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights to a licensee but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain exclusionary rights—specifically the right to sue third parties for infringement—satisfy the irreducible constitutional minimum of standing even after granting an exclusive license. The court analyzed the license agreement's provisions on shared enforcement control, sublicensing approval rights, and retained use rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure license agreements to retain enforcement rights and maintain standing to sue infringers, even after granting broad exclusive licenses. This preserves flexibility in patent monetization and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face a broader pool of potential plaintiffs, as this decision makes it harder to defeat patent suits on standing grounds where the patent owner has retained any meaningful exclusionary right.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that includes a single infringement question covering multiple asserted patents is reversible error, and whether the district court erred in its Alice step two analysis for a patent directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the single-question verdict form covering all asserted patents was improper because it prevented meaningful appellate review. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings under Alice step two for the '495 patent while affirming that the '887 and '371 patents survived Alice step one.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement benefit from the requirement that verdict forms separately identify which patents are infringed, preventing plaintiffs from obtaining aggregate verdicts that obscure potentially invalid or non-infringed patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased litigation complexity and risk of retrial when asserting multiple patents, as courts must now ensure verdict forms allow for patent-by-patent findings on infringement and damages.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) had expired before Insulet brought suit, and when a plaintiff knew or should have known of trade secret misappropriation for limitations purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and damages award for trade secret misappropriation, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred as a matter of law. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit, based on evidence that former employees had shared confidential CAD files and design information with the competitor.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation gain a strong precedent for enforcing the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, particularly when the plaintiff had early awareness of the alleged misconduct but delayed filing suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering potential misappropriation or risk losing their federal DTSA claims entirely. Companies that adopt a wait-and-see approach to monitor competitor products before suing may find their claims time-barred.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar invalidity defenses that were not raised in the IPR petition but allegedly could have been discovered through a reasonably diligent search.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding that the lower court relied on insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias when estopping another. The decision limits the scope of estoppel that can be imposed on IPR petitioners in subsequent district court litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies that file IPR petitions benefit from a more nuanced estoppel standard that guards against hindsight bias and requires robust evidence before barring invalidity defenses not raised in the IPR. This preserves the ability to raise additional prior art in district court.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a more limited application of IPR estoppel, meaning defendants may raise additional invalidity arguments in district court even after an IPR, potentially prolonging and complicating patent litigation.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of the jury's breach of contract award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The case arose from Ford's development of competing software after licensing Versata's automotive configuration tools.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from broader acceptance of damages methodologies and the reinstatement of jury damage awards. The decision signals that trial courts should not be overly restrictive in excluding expert damages testimony.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies that develop in-house alternatives to licensed software face increased exposure to trade secret misappropriation damages, as the court expanded the range of permissible damages models that plaintiffs can present.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-provisional patent application's change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in a substituent definition was an obvious typographical error correction that preserved priority to the provisional application, or constituted impermissible new matter.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that Enanta's '953 patent could not claim priority to its provisional application because the change from C2 to C1 in the alkyl range was not an obvious typographical error. Without provisional priority, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (the active ingredient in Paxlovid®) anticipated the patent claims. This decision effectively cleared a patent obstacle to generic competition for COVID-19 treatments.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies and competitors benefit from strict enforcement of priority requirements, ensuring that patent applicants cannot retroactively broaden claims through alleged typographical error corrections after a competitor's disclosure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators face significant risk that even minor drafting errors in provisional applications can result in loss of priority and patent invalidation, emphasizing the critical importance of meticulous provisional application drafting.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'dextromethorphan' in a pharmaceutical patent's weight-to-weight ratio limitation refers to the free base form or the salt form of the compound, and whether a district court may waive the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal of a preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's preliminary injunction blocking a generic competitor from launching a Nuedexta generic, upholding the claim construction that the weight-to-weight ratio limitation refers to the free base forms of dextromethorphan and quinidine. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, requiring the patent holder to post security pending appeal.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies gain protection from at-risk generic launches through preliminary injunctions, with the court endorsing claim constructions that cover salt-form generic products under free-base claim language.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug companies face delayed market entry, and the bond requirement ensures that patent holders bear financial risk if the injunction is ultimately found improper. The ruling on bond waiver establishes that even strong cases require security.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of patent claims directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in drug-eluting coronary stent systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's infringement verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement. The court found that prior art anticipated the asserted claims of the '296 patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable polymer fiber compositions used in coronary stents. The decision eliminated a significant damages award.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers gain significant protection from this ruling, which raised the bar for patent holders asserting broad composition claims against established stent technologies. The reversal removes potential royalty obligations on widely used coronary stent products.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and research institutions face heightened challenges in enforcing broad composition patents against major medical device companies, particularly when prior art closely aligns with claimed inventions.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for tracking farming operations using GPS, implement profiles, and automated data recording are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's refusal to find the case exceptional under § 285 should be reviewed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under § 101, finding the claims recite the abstract idea of collecting, processing, and sharing farming data. However, the court vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorney's fees under § 285.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies and data platform providers benefit from the invalidation of broad data-collection patents, reducing the risk of infringement claims for precision agriculture products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the agtech space face continued difficulty in obtaining and enforcing patents on data collection and processing systems, and the remand on exceptionality signals increased risk of fee-shifting for asserting weak patents.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's under-protest determination that debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit, and whether Commerce's original equityworthiness analysis should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and instructed it to reinstate Commerce's original determinations that three debt-to-equity conversions by a Korean steel company conferred countervailable subsidies. The court found that Commerce's original analysis—finding the company was not equityworthy at the time of the government-provided equity infusions—was supported by the record and should not have been overturned on remand.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and other industries subject to foreign subsidized competition benefit from the reinstatement of countervailing duty determinations, strengthening trade remedy protections against government-subsidized equity infusions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers face reimposition of countervailing duties based on original Commerce determinations, increasing costs and potentially disrupting established supply chains.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss patent infringement claims with prejudice on obviousness grounds at the pleading stage based on a prior IPR decision invalidating other claims of the same patent, and whether filing such a suit warrants exceptional case fees under § 285 or attorney sanctions under § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of patent infringement claims where the asserted claims were found obvious on the same grounds that invalidated other claims in a prior IPR. However, the court reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award against the plaintiff and the § 1927 sanctions against counsel, finding insufficient evidence of bad faith or exceptionality.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses defending against patent suits benefit from the precedent allowing dismissal at the pleading stage when surviving IPR claims are obvious on the same grounds. However, the reversal of fee-shifting limits the ability to recover defense costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that claims surviving IPR may still be dismissed at the pleading stage. The reversal of sanctions, however, protects patent plaintiffs from the chilling effect of automatic fee awards for filing suits involving weakened patents.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim limitations reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform specified functions in software patents invoke means-plus-function treatment under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), and whether the Dyfan framework applies retroactively to pending cases.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling regarding the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration under the intervening Dyfan precedent, which clarified when software claim limitations invoke § 112(f) means-plus-function treatment. The court affirmed the invalidity judgment on the '638 patent for anticipation under § 102.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the opportunity to have their claims reconsidered under the more nuanced Dyfan framework, potentially saving patents from indefiniteness invalidation based on pre-Dyfan analysis.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against software patents face continued uncertainty about whether functional claim language invokes § 112(f), potentially prolonging litigation through remands for new claim construction proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Wyeth LLC v. AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to methods of treating gefitinib/erlotinib-resistant non-small cell lung cancer using irreversible EGFR inhibitors are invalid for lack of enablement or written description support, and whether JMOL of invalidity was appropriate.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed JMOL of invalidity for Wyeth's cancer treatment method patents asserted against AstraZeneca, finding that the broadly claimed methods of treating g/e-resistant NSCLC with any irreversible EGFR inhibitor were not adequately supported. The decision cleared patent obstacles for AstraZeneca's competing oncology products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical companies developing competing cancer treatments benefit from the removal of broad method-of-treatment patent claims, enabling continued commercialization of irreversible EGFR inhibitors without infringement risk.
impacts.negativeImplications: Innovators holding broad method-of-treatment patents face heightened scrutiny of enablement and written description, particularly when claims encompass genus-level compounds with limited species disclosed in the specification.
